primary_cause: Macro tech selloff tied to COVID supply-chain and demand fears. Apple earlier supply warning read-through for semis
secondary_factors: Lingering China manufacturing disruption and broad de-risking in semis. 10-year briefly ~0.318% on Mar 9. No material Intel-specific announcement
store_description: Intel's drop looks less like an Intel event and more like a semiconductor and hardware repricing as investors digested the Saudi-Russia oil shock the 10-year yield briefly touching about 0.318% on March 9 and WHO pandemic declaration on March 11.

primary_cause: Global recession fears hitting cyclicals. Energy capex pressure after crude roughly 25% plunge on Mar 9
secondary_factors: Construction mining and energy spending exposure. No CAT-specific announcement in prior 3 days
store_description: Caterpillar traded like a pure macro industrial on March 11 because its earnings power is highly tied to commodity construction and equipment demand. With crude suffering its biggest daily rout since the Gulf War the market marked down heavy-equipment demand expectations.

primary_cause: Bank-sector repricing on lower rates plus expected credit losses. 10-year crashed toward 0.318%
secondary_factors: Funding and liquidity fear and broad risk-off selling in financials. No Citi-specific corporate announcement
store_description: Citi's larger drop versus the S&P fits how banks were hit when the 10-year yield crashed toward 0.318% and investors started discounting both net-interest-margin compression and future loan losses from a virus-driven recession. Sector move first not Citi-specific.

primary_cause: Mark-to-market fear around Berkshire portfolio and operating subsidiaries. Large exposure to economically sensitive holdings especially financials and airlines
secondary_factors: Airline exposure and broad financial-sector weakness. No Berkshire corporate announcement
store_description: Berkshire sold off less violently than airlines or banks themselves but the market was still repricing its look-through exposure to holdings like American Express Bank of America Wells Fargo and the airlines as COVID worsened. BRK-B was trading as a diversified macro proxy.

primary_cause: Expected AUM and fee pressure from market turmoil. Extreme market volatility threatened AUM levels and fee revenue
secondary_factors: Broad financial-sector derating and ETF and flow uncertainty during the crash. No BlackRock-specific negative
store_description: BlackRock's stock was hit because its revenue base was levered to asset values just as global equities were plunging again on March 11. This was mainly a business-model-through-the-cycle selloff rather than a company-specific event.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Booking withdrew Q1 2020 guidance on Mar 9 due to worsening COVID impact on travel demand. IATA warned Mar 5 airlines could lose $63B-$113B passenger revenue
secondary_factors: Rapidly worsening global travel restrictions and broader market panic
store_description: This one had a clear stock-specific trigger. On March 9 Booking formally pulled its first-quarter guidance directly citing the worsening effect of COVID-19 on travel demand. The broader travel complex was already under pressure from IATA's $63B-$113B airline revenue-loss warning.

primary_cause: Rates and recession-driven financials selloff. Fee pressure on lower asset values and lower net interest revenue
secondary_factors: Market-value pressure on custody and AUM-linked fees. No BNY Mellon-specific announcement
store_description: BK traded like a rate-sensitive financial whose earnings would be hit from both sides: lower interest income and lower market-linked fee revenue as asset prices fell. No obvious company-specific shock so the move looks overwhelmingly sector and macro driven.

primary_cause: Lower rates and expected credit deterioration. Treasury yield collapse oil-shock recession fears
secondary_factors: General banking-sector derating. No fresh Bank of America-specific announcement. Milder than Citi
store_description: BAC's decline was milder than Citi's but the logic was the same: with the 10-year yield plunging and investors contemplating a deep COVID recession banks were repriced for weaker loan growth lower margins and future credit losses.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Boeing said Mar 11 freezing new hiring and most overtime to preserve cash as COVID compounded 737 MAX damage
secondary_factors: Collapsing airline demand. IATA warned $63B-$113B passenger revenue loss. Sector-wide fears about aircraft orders and cancellations
store_description: BA had the clearest company-specific negative. On the same day Boeing announced a hiring and overtime freeze to conserve cash explicitly tying the move to COVID on top of the 737 MAX crisis. Investors extrapolated weaker deliveries more order risk and more liquidity pressure.

primary_cause: No Colgate-specific negative. Broad equity de-risking. Smaller drop than cyclicals fits defensive staples profile
secondary_factors: Supply-chain uncertainty and defensive-stock selling to raise cash
store_description: Colgate's drop was smaller than many cyclical names which fits the idea that it was mostly being dragged by the tape rather than by an idiosyncratic shock. In a liquidation-style session even defensive staples were sold.

primary_cause: Expected collapse in travel-and-entertainment card spending. IATA warned Mar 5 of $63B-$113B airline revenue hit
secondary_factors: Recession fear and rising consumer-credit risk. No AXP corporate release in prior 3 days. Travel-payments hybrid move
store_description: American Express was especially vulnerable because of its business-travel and T&E exposure so the market discounted a faster hit to billed business than for generic lenders. The March 11 selloff looks less like a plain financials move and more like a travel-payments hybrid move.

primary_cause: No meaningful American Tower-specific negative. Broad market liquidation. Temporary factor unwind
secondary_factors: Concern that tenant financing and global rollout activity could slow in a pandemic
store_description: AMT's decline looks like a correlation trade rather than a reaction to a tower-industry development. In a stress event investors sold liquid long-duration equities broadly including high-quality REITs that had no immediate company-specific bad news.

primary_cause: No major Amgen-specific negative. Broad March 11 risk-off after WHO pandemic declaration
secondary_factors: Biotech and pharma basket selling despite relative defensiveness
store_description: Amgen's smaller decline versus most cyclicals suggests it was partly cushioned by defensive characteristics but it still got dragged lower with the index. No evidence of an Amgen-specific catalyst in the 3-day window.

primary_cause: Semiconductor capital-equipment selloff on COVID uncertainty. Apple earlier warning primed market
secondary_factors: Hardware supply-chain disruption and global capex fears. Fabs could delay deliveries and capex. No Applied Materials-specific negative
store_description: AMAT moved more than Intel because equipment names were exposed not just to end-demand risk but also to the possibility that fabs and supply chains would delay deliveries and capex. The market was already primed by Apple's earlier warning.

primary_cause: Pre-earnings derisking inside marketwide growth-stock selloff. Due to report earnings Mar 12. No fresh Adobe-specific negative
secondary_factors: Concern that business spending would slow sharply. High-multiple software names being sold on fear of weaker corporate budgets
store_description: Adobe's decline appears driven by valuation compression and earnings-event caution rather than an Adobe-specific bombshell. In that environment high-multiple software names were being sold on fear that corporate budgets and advertising-related activity would weaken.

primary_cause: Expected slowdown in consulting and discretionary client spending. Later warned Mar 19 coronavirus would pressure quarterly revenue
secondary_factors: Broad market de-rating of services firms exposed to enterprise budgets. No Accenture-specific release in prior 3 days
store_description: ACN traded as a high-quality but economically exposed services company whose clients could postpone transformation and consulting projects in a sudden downturn. The subsequent March 19 revenue warning supports the view that March 11 was the market front-running a real earnings headwind.

primary_cause: No Abbott-specific negative. EUA for molecular COVID test not until Mar 18. Broad market liquidation
secondary_factors: Temporary healthcare basket selling despite later test-related upside. Relatively modest decline fits more defensive name
store_description: Abbott's relatively modest decline fits a name that was more defensive than average but still could not escape a tape-driven selloff. The absence of a negative company catalyst combined with the later positive March 18 test authorization suggests this was macro pressure.

primary_cause: No meaningful AbbVie-specific negative. Allergan acquisition still pending. Marketwide selling
secondary_factors: General risk-off and merger-arbitrage and financing sensitivity
store_description: AbbVie's small decline relative to the market looks like generalized liquidation rather than a targeted reassessment. Without a new AbbVie headline in the window the simplest explanation is broad de-risking with some extra caution around large-deal financing.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Already warned Feb 18 would miss March-quarter revenue guidance due to COVID supply and demand damage. Tim Cook allowed most staff to work from home
secondary_factors: Broad tech selloff and continued concern about slow supply-chain normalization. Supply chains recovering more slowly than hoped
store_description: Apple's March 11 decline was not caused by a brand-new filing but was still highly stock-specific in the sense that investors were repricing a name that had already admitted virus-related revenue damage. Reports that tech supply chains were recovering more slowly than hoped reinforced the fear.

primary_cause: No materially negative Amazon-specific announcement. Broad mega-cap tech selloff
secondary_factors: Uncertainty around logistics and labor disruption versus higher e-commerce demand. Both positives and negatives from COVID
store_description: Amazon's decline looks more like index-level and growth-stock de-risking than a reaction to a specific Amazon negative. Unlike travel or airlines Amazon had both positives and negatives from COVID so the stock's March 11 move appears mostly tied to the market's second-leg selloff.
